knowledgeSummary:
You've been building out a detailed strategic picture of Nike, and it's rich enough now to read almost like a full case study rather than scattered notes.

**The market wasn't sized, it was widened.** Bowerman's "if you have a body, you're an athlete" line, and Knight's willingness to claim a billion-dollar market when the real number was $2 billion, both point to the same move: Nike didn't discover demand, it redefined who counts as a customer until the market caught up.

**The founding constraint became the culture.** Impossible unit economics on Tigers, a banker who wouldn't lend against growth, and a 100% debt-to-assets ratio weren't choices so much as survival tactics, yet they hardened into Nike's permanent growth orientation, even now with $10.7 billion in cash sitting against that old identity.

**Scale, not brand, is the real moat.** You've landed on a sharp distinction: Nike doesn't out-margin Adidas, it out-volumes it. The Kobe story (paying to leave Adidas) shows the mechanism, bigger athlete platform attracts bigger stars attracts bigger platform, a loop small rivals like Under Armour can't replicate no matter how much they spend.

**The unresolved tension.** Knight himself called Nike a marketing company that happens to sell shoes as its best marketing tool, and you've flagged the counter-read: maybe the athletes are the product and the shoe is just the monetization. That question sits unanswered at the center of everything else, including live risks, women's underdevelopment, resale value walked away from, and running fragmenting under Nike from On and Hoka.

This is dense, well-covered ground. Where it'd be worth pushing next is turning the Nike pattern into a live decision, what would *your* version of "widening the definition" or "scale through talent" actually look like applied elsewhere.

suggestedQuestions.title: Product company or marketing company?
suggestedQuestions.description: Knight said Nike is a marketing company with the product as its best marketing tool, but the material also argues the athletes are the real product and the shoe just monetizes them. Which framing would you actually build a strategy on, and does it change what gets invested in next?

suggestedQuestions.title: What breaks the scale loop?
suggestedQuestions.description: The Kobe mechanism, bigger platform attracts bigger stars attracts bigger platform, is presented as durable, but On, Hoka and Brooks are already taking share in running by ignoring that loop entirely. What would it take for a competitor to break the loop rather than just fund a smaller copy of it?

suggestedQuestions.title: Is women's the next Jordan?
suggestedQuestions.description: Women's is called the clearest underdeveloped segment even while it's already bigger than all of Lululemon. What would it actually take to build a women's equivalent of the Jordan mechanism, rather than treating it as a product-line gap to fill?

decisionStack.vision: If you have a body, you are an athlete
decisionStack.visionElaboration: Bowerman said it in 1965 when running wasn't even a sport, and it is still the widest definition of a customer anyone in this industry has written down. Every person alive should be able to reach the top of what Nike makes, whatever they do with their body.
decisionStack.strategy: Buy the world's athletes, spend more than anyone can match creating demand, then sell at everyone else's price to win volume
decisionStack.strategyElaboration: Athletes are the asset. The product is how someone buys into what they just watched. We spend $4 billion a year on demand creation because scale is the only advantage that holds in a category with no lock-in, no network effect and shoes that wear out. We deliberately leave money on the table, at retail prices we could raise and in a resale market we could capture, because maximum swooshes in the world is worth more than the margin.

fragments.title: The addressable market is defined as everyone with a body
fragments.content:
Bill Bowerman's line — that anyone with a body is an athlete — is the founding definition of Nike's market, and it was radical when written. In 1965 running was not a sport, not popular, not unpopular; it simply was, and people mocked runners from car windows. Bowerman's 1967 book Jogging and the Life magazine profile that followed helped start the American fitness movement outright. The company did not find a large market so much as widen the definition of who counts as a customer until the market became large.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: But everyone's an athlete, he said. If you have a body, then you're an athlete.
In 1965, running wasn't even a sport. It wasn't popular. It wasn't unpopular. It just was.

fragments.title: Scale today, and the shape of the customer base
fragments.content:
Nike is a $51 billion revenue business growing about 10% a year — the largest apparel company in the world outside luxury. Footwear is roughly three times apparel by revenue. On a wholesale-equivalent basis men's is 51%, women's 21%, kids' 12%, with Jordan a separate 16%. Including Jordan, roughly 64% of product goes to men. The structure of the customer base has changed far less since the IPO than the scale has.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: They are a $51 billion revenue business growing 10% year over year.
Men's is 51%, women's is 21%, kids' is 12%, and the Jordan brand broken out separately.

fragments.title: Women are the largest underserved segment inside the business
fragments.content:
Nike's sales to women alone exceed all of Lululemon's revenue — and yet at $8.6 billion of a $50 billion business, women's is the clearest under-developed segment. Both facts are true at once, which is the point: a segment can be enormous in absolute terms and still be the biggest gap in the portfolio. Nike has lagged on product development for women relative to its position everywhere else.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike sales to women alone are bigger than all of Lululemon's revenue.
It's just $8.6 billion of their $50 billion of revenue.

fragments.title: Near-monopoly in basketball, the category that converts to everyday wear
fragments.content:
Nike and Jordan held 86% of performance basketball and 96% of lifestyle basketball before the pandemic. Basketball matters disproportionately because its shoes are wearable off the court — the observation that only running, basketball and tennis really matter, since those are the only shoes ordinary people wear. Football and soccer generate enormous attention but almost nothing a spectator can buy and wear.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike and the Air Jordan brand's share of performance basketball was 86%.
running, basketball, and tennis are the only sports that matter because those are the only shoes that normal people can wear

fragments.title: A replacement market of fourteen billion feet
fragments.content:
The branded athletic shoe market in the US alone is roughly $130 billion, growing about 5% a year — larger than the video game market. The underlying appeal is that everyone wears shoes and shoes wear out, producing recurring demand without any subscription mechanism. Nike helped create the world in which sneakers are worn all day rather than only for sport, then sells into it.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: The branded athletic shoe market in the US today is $130 billion.
Not everybody has to play video games, but everybody's got to wear shoes.

fragments.title: Sneakers became identity, and a secondary market followed
fragments.content:
Shoes became a method of self-expression rather than equipment, and a resale market of somewhere between $2 billion and $6 billion grew up around limited releases. Nike has deliberately declined to capture it — shoes sold at $150-$300 trade instantly for thousands on StockX and GOAT. The reading offered is that this is the price of keeping the dream attainable, since the marketing strategy targets tastemakers in a dozen global cities who are not wealthy.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Shoes had become this method for self-expression.
That is a very intentional decision by Nike not to capture that value.

fragments.title: The founding insight was manufacturing arbitrage, borrowed from cameras
fragments.content:
Phil Knight's Stanford business plan applied a pattern he had watched in photography: German incumbents like Leica being undercut by Japanese entrants such as Nikon at far lower prices. Athletic footwear had the identical structure, with Adidas and Puma dominant and Converse stranded in the canvas era. The insight was not about shoes at all — it was that the same low-end disruption would repeat in a second industry.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: He knows from the photography department that high-end professional cameras had traditionally been the domain of the Germans.
okay, this is a good idea to apply Japanese low end disruption to the athletic apparel market and the footwear market, but this is not a big market

fragments.title: The market was correctly judged too small — and the judgement was irrelevant
fragments.content:
Knight's classmates and faculty were unimpressed because the market genuinely was small: US running shoes were perhaps $100 million, all branded athletic shoes about $2 billion. Knight claimed a billion dollars in a meeting, with no evidence. He was wrong in both directions — wrong about the market then, and far more wrong about what it would become, since it is now roughly $130 billion. Sizing the market as it existed would have killed the idea.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: He tells them that he's done market research. He thinks that the US track shoe, running shoe market could be a $1 billion market, which he totally makes up.
He's also completely wrong on what it would become in the other direction.

fragments.title: The original business had no product and no defensibility
fragments.content:
Blue Ribbon Sports began as pure importing and reselling — not Nike, no swoosh, no product of its own. The judgement offered is that this was more defensible then than it would be now: proprietary distribution in a geography, built by driving to track meets, was a real asset before the internet and venture capital made scale instantaneous. The company started with the thinnest possible claim to value and built everything else on top.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: It's literally just importing and reselling someone else's product. The plan is to build a big business off the back of not actually making things.
That's legitimately doing the shoe leather work that no one else is willing to do

fragments.title: The gross margin never penciled, which forced everything else
fragments.content:
Tigers sold for $6.95 against roughly $3.50 of cost, and about $1.75 of what remained went to sales commissions — leaving perhaps $2 a pair. Reordering inventory at $3.50 out of $2 of profit is arithmetically impossible. This is described as a circular problem with no internal solution, and it is what pushed the company into the financing structures that shaped its character.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Phil is selling the Tigers for $6.95 a pair. It costs him and Bowerman about $3.50 to get each pair of shoes.
How are you going to order more inventory at $3.50 a pair when you're making $2 in profit per pair? The math doesn't pencil.

fragments.title: Banks could not value a company that had no assets
fragments.content:
Knight's banker treated 100% annual sales growth as a warning sign, because lending was against book value only. The concept of enterprise value effectively did not exist for a small company: you could borrow roughly what you already had, which is a cash advance rather than capital. Asking for a $1.2 million line of credit got him thrown out. The constraint was not Nike's business model but the financial system it was born into.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Your rate of growth is too fast for your equity, he said. Growth off your balance sheet is dangerous.
it's almost as if the idea of enterprise value didn't exist, that literally a company it could only possibly be thought of as its assets minus liabilities.

fragments.title: The equity route failed, including a rename to sound like tech
fragments.content:
Before finding Japanese trading companies, Knight attempted a small local share offering and renamed the company Sports-Tek Inc so it would sound like a technology business. Nobody bought. He fell back on convertible notes from employees' families — Bob Woodell's family lent a few thousand dollars, an enormous share of their net worth, which later converted and made them millionaires. Nothing about the early financing was orthodox because nothing orthodox was available.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: He changes the name of the company to Sports-Tek Inc with the idea that, oh, this will make us sound like a technology company, and then people will be interested in investing.
The offering fails. Nobody's interested.

fragments.title: Growth as a survival requirement, not an ambition
fragments.content:
Knight ran at or near a 100% debt-to-assets ratio deliberately, matching debt to whatever assets existed so as to grow as fast as possible. That leverage makes growth compulsory: inventory has to sell fast enough to repay the bank so the next loan can be drawn. The observation drawn is that Nike's growth orientation — still declared at the top of its investor relations page — originated as the only way to keep the lights on.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: You literally need growth as the only way to keep the lights on. It's not just growth as a virtue. It's growth as a necessity.
Nike Inc is a growth company

fragments.title: The product is a way to participate in the dream
fragments.content:
The stated mechanism is that athletes function as billboards and the products are how a spectator buys into what they saw. Nobody is expected to buy the exact shoe an athlete wears; the athlete sells the swoosh, and the customer buys a product built for their own life. Nike's income statement calls the spending 'demand creation', which is a precise description of the model.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: It's about getting you to buy Nike.
You're buying victory.

fragments.title: Genuine performance innovation underwrites the aspiration
fragments.content:
The credibility rests on innovation that measurably works: Bowerman's waffle sole, Air cushioning, Flyknit, and the Vaporfly, which is described as provably making a runner 4% faster and prompted debate about banning it. The Vaporfly was for two years plainly the best running shoe available. Real advantage in the pinnacle product is what makes the aspirational layer credible rather than merely asserted.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike stages this event with their shoes that provably make you 4% faster than you've ever been before.
it was by far the best running shoe on the market for two whole years

fragments.title: Brand power that shows up as consideration, not price
fragments.content:
Nike does not charge more than its competitors — its running shoes sit at the same $160-$180 as Adidas or New Balance, and Adidas has posted a higher gross margin every quarter for a decade. So the brand advantage does not appear as a price premium in Helmer's sense. It appears as never looking at the alternative, which converts to volume rather than margin.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: It shows up in the fact that I often don't look at a competitor. I will only go by the Nike thing.
Adidas, every single quarter for the last 10 years has had a higher gross margin.

fragments.title: The premium is deliberately left on the table
fragments.content:
There is essentially nothing Nike sells for $500, despite producing many items worth multiples of that on resale. The conclusion drawn is that this is a choice rather than an inability, made so the brand stays accessible to the young tastemakers in the dozen cities Nike orients its marketing around — people who cannot spend thousands but must be able to reach the pinnacle of the brand.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: I don't think there is anything that I can buy from Nike that cost $500.
they have to keep it attainable

fragments.title: Two different products under one swoosh
fragments.content:
The line splits: prestige models — Jordans, retros, Vaporfly at $150 and above — are genuinely differentiated products, while the high-volume $50-$70 shoes are commodities carried by the brand halo. The Monarch, a shoe no athlete has ever competed in, has been among the best sellers. Both halves are necessary, and conflating them is how the business gets misread.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: I think those are products. Nike also sells a lot of $50, $60, $70 pairs of shoes. Those are probably commodities that are helped by the brand halo.
The Monarchs are objectively a commodity product.

fragments.title: Knight's own account, and the disagreement with it
fragments.content:
Asked directly whether Nike is a product company or a marketing company, Phil Knight said it is a marketing company and the product is its most important marketing tool. The counter-argument offered is that the athletes are the marketing tool and the product is the monetisation of it — but admitting that would be admitting the product is not the differentiator. The tension is unresolved and sits at the centre of the whole business.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: We are a marketing company, and the product is our most important marketing tool.
I think the product is a monetization method for the marketing that you do through athletes.

fragments.title: A power law unlike the rest of apparel
fragments.content:
Nike is more than twice the size of Adidas, which is more than three times the next player. No other corner of the apparel industry — shirts, trousers, jackets — concentrates like this. Two or three companies make a huge share of all the sneakers in the world, and that structural concentration is what makes scale economies the operative power here rather than brand.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: today, Nike is more than twice the size of Adidas, who is more than three times, I think, the size of the number three player
There are two, three, four companies that make a huge share of all of the sneakers that the world wears, that's wild.

fragments.title: No switching costs and no network effects
fragments.content:
Footwear has no lock-in of any kind. Customers change brands freely, there is no network benefit to others wearing Nike, and there is no cornered resource. Whatever durability exists has to be continuously repurchased through innovation and brand investment — which is precisely why the marketing spend can never stop.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: I frequently switch shoe brands all the time.
there's no potential for any form of lock-in, and there's no potential for really any form of network effects

fragments.title: The Jordan deal was counter-positioning the incumbents could not copy
fragments.content:
Converse paid Magic Johnson and Larry Bird roughly $100,000 a year in cash for a non-signature shoe. Nike offered Jordan a signature line plus a 5% royalty on gross revenue — a structure Converse could not match, because its existing stars would never tolerate a newcomer getting fundamentally better terms. Nike could offer upside precisely because it had nothing to lose; its competitors had too much.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Their deals were roughly $100,000 a year in cash payments to wear the Converse Weapons.
the payouts were calculated as a 5% royalty on gross revenue from the sales of Air Jordans, the whole line, the shoes, the merchandise, everything

fragments.title: Reebok overtook Nike by serving a market Nike refused on principle
fragments.content:
Reebok was founded in 1980 and had passed Nike in sales by 1988, at over a billion dollars. It won with an aerobics shoe Nike considered bad — soft wrinkled white leather that went well with legwarmers, which women loved. Nike had mistaken the running boom, a cyclical fad, for the fitness boom, a secular trend, and declined to make aerobics shoes as a matter of principle. Refusing a market on aesthetic grounds nearly cost the company its lead.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: In 1980, Reebok USA is founded. By 1988, Reebok eclipses Nike in sales.
They mistook the running and the jogging boom for the broader fitness boom.

fragments.title: Adidas has repeatedly lost on its own strategy
fragments.content:
Adidas pursues eyeballs rather than athletes — rappers, musicians, celebrities — and the Yeezy collapse took its profit from over $2 billion a year to under $100 million on a rolling basis, with an actual quarterly loss. Nike had walked away from Kanye in 2015 over creative control. The contrast presented is that an athlete-only roster is narrower but far more defensible, because Nike knows what it is celebrating.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Adidas net income has basically evaporated and gone to zero. They used to make over $2 billion a year in profit.
our entire brand is built on celebrating athletes

fragments.title: The danger of being caught in the middle
fragments.content:
Under Armour is offered as the cautionary case: it pays Steph Curry enormous sums and equity while running a miniature version of the Nike playbook without the scale that playbook requires. The prescription is to be either the platform brand or the focused niche — Nike or Brooks — but not a small company executing a large company's strategy.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: don't get caught in the middle in the age of the Internet
They don't have the size, scale, and everything that accrues to a Nike, but they're trying to run a mini Nike playbook.

fragments.title: Niche competitors are winning in the founding category
fragments.content:
On, Hoka and Brooks have each become billion-dollar businesses in running — the category Nike was born in — by focusing on the trainers people actually wear week to week rather than race-day shoes. Nike has been protected less by its own performance than by Adidas being, as put, out to lunch. The threat is fragmentation from below in the one category that historically signalled the company's health.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: You've got Brooks on and Hoka all becoming billion dollar revenue run great companies in the last 18 months.
Nike, fortunately, their big competitors like Adidas have just been out to lunch.

fragments.title: A fabless shoe company
fragments.content:
Nike does over $50 billion in revenue without making a single shoe — the analogy drawn is to fabless semiconductors. The differences matter: shoe manufacturing is not capital-intensive the way a fab is and carries little process power, so the foundry-equivalent ecosystem is fragmented rather than concentrated. The one exception is telling — Nike manufactures 100% of its own nitrogen-filled air units, in Oregon, because that is trade secret, then ships them to Asia for assembly.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: They're a fabless shoe company.
Nike manufacture zero shoes, but they manufacture 100% of the nitrogen-filled little air bags.

fragments.title: Margins that are good, and nothing like luxury
fragments.content:
Gross margin runs about 44% against LVMH at 68% and Hermes at 71%; operating income is $6.4 billion on $51 billion, a 12.5% operating margin. Real materials, labour, logistics and inventory costs sit underneath. Better than a car company, well short of luxury, and nowhere near software — which is the honest frame for a company often discussed as though it were a luxury house.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike is better than a car company, but it ain't no luxury.
Nike does $6.4 billion in operating income, so that's their income before taxes, 12½% operating margin.

fragments.title: The Futures Program moved financing onto retailers
fragments.content:
Scarred by the banks, Knight offered retailers a 7% discount to commit and pay six months ahead — shifting working capital from lenders onto customers. Retailers refused until the waffle trainer became unobtainable any other way. It also worked as a shock absorber: because orders were locked six months out, revenue barely declined during the Reebok years even as the underlying business deteriorated.

He's essentially moving his financing from banks and Nissho Iwai over to his retail partners, to his customers.

fragments.title: The trading company that made everything possible
fragments.content:
Nissho Iwai — a $100 billion revenue Japanese trading company — financed all of Blue Ribbon's inventory at market rates, introduced it to Japanese factories so it could make its own shoes, and took a 4% royalty on every shoe sold, on top of interest. The relationship ran for thirty or forty years. It also carried real risk: these firms routinely ended up controlling the businesses they financed, which is what Knight negotiated against.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nissho gets a 4% royalty on every shoe that Blue Ribbon sells, which ultimately ends up being a great relationship.
It's a hybrid between a lender and a supply chain partner

fragments.title: The Jordan deal economics, and what they actually paid
fragments.content:
A $2.5 million minimum guarantee over five years, structured as a 5% royalty on gross Jordan revenue, plus a royalty on incremental Nike basketball sales above the prior year's 400,000 pairs, a guaranteed advertising commitment and stock options. In year one Jordan earned $6.3 million — exactly his entire seven-year Bulls contract. The renegotiation in year three raised the guarantee to $18 million.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: The deal is a $2½ million minimum guaranteed payout over five years, but that's not actually how the economics work.
That's $6.3 million that Jordan got from Nike in 1985.

fragments.title: Jordan as a compounding annuity long after retirement
fragments.content:
Jordan brand did $6.6 billion in FY22 and has grown about 35% a year for three years while Nike overall grows 10% — making it the fastest-growing part of the company. At a 5% royalty that is over $300 million a year to a man who retired twenty years ago, plausibly $5-10 billion across his life. Nike keeps the other 95% and is entirely content with the arrangement.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: This past year, they just reported, FY22, the Jordan brand did $6.6 billion in revenue.
There is no athlete making $300 million a year.

fragments.title: From capital-starved to not knowing what to do with cash
fragments.content:
The company that once ran at a 100% debt-to-assets ratio now holds $10.7 billion in cash alongside $8.5 billion of inventory, and has raised its dividend for thirty consecutive quarters. Knight raised $22 million at IPO and essentially never needed more. The complete inversion of the founding constraint sits oddly against the growth-company self-description.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: they also, in addition to that inventory, have $10.7 billion in cash and similar equivalents
They've now had 30 consecutive quarters of increasing dividend payouts.

fragments.title: Never taking dilution is how the founder ended up owning half of it
fragments.content:
Because every round of growth was funded with debt rather than equity, Knight, his management team and Bowerman held 56% at IPO, Knight alone 46%. He was worth $178 million on IPO day and roughly $40 billion now. The leverage that nearly destroyed the company repeatedly is the same decision that preserved the ownership.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Phil Knight basically never took on any equity investors, so he took no dilution.
He shot the moon, and he kept ownership the whole way.

fragments.title: Sports marketing was effectively invented to get around amateurism rules
fragments.content:
Steve Prefontaine could not accept endorsements under amateur athletics rules, so Nike employed him as National Director of Public Affairs for $5,000 a year with no duties. Knight's explanation of the role was that it meant he could run fast. It is the origin of athlete endorsement as practised today, and it was a rule-avoidance manoeuvre before it was a marketing strategy.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: What Phil does is he decides to employ Pre as a corporate employee of Nike, as the National Director of Public Affairs for $5000 a year.
People asked me what that meant. I said, it means he can run fast.

fragments.title: Buying the middle of the market rather than the stars
fragments.content:
Rob Strasser signed roughly half the NBA — not the stars but the journeymen and role players — for close to nothing beyond free shoes, putting the swoosh on national broadcasts every night. The same logic drove the college programme: Sonny Vaccaro signed coaches as consultants, since nothing prevented a coach being paid, and the coach then set team footwear policy. Cheap, systematic, and entirely about impressions rather than the shoes sold.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: He signs up half the NBA for peanuts, not the big stars, but the journeyman, the role players in the NBA.
Strasser gets Sonny to go around the country and sign up coaches of the big basketball schools to become Nike coaches.

fragments.title: Athletes are content, and scale buys the content
fragments.content:
The framing offered is that athletes function the way Netflix shows do — Nike acquires them, and the biggest customer base can pay the most, which attracts the best athletes, which grows the customer base. Kobe bought his way out of Adidas reportedly for $8 million to join Nike, because what Nike could do for him exceeded what a smaller platform could. This is the mechanism by which scale economies, not brand, become the operative power.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: The whole game, just like Netflix, is Nike is acquiring content.
Athletes are Netflix shows.

fragments.title: $4 billion a year, booked as demand creation
fragments.content:
The marketing line on the financial statements is literally called demand creation, which is an unusually candid description: buying media to manufacture demand for products. At $4 billion a year it is a scale weapon smaller competitors cannot match, and it is the reason the growth question is never simply about reinvesting more cash.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: They already spend $4 billion a year on demand creation.
we're basically going out and buying media to create demand for our products

fragments.title: Paying to be a billboard on jerseys someone else sells
fragments.content:
Nike pays roughly $200 million a year to be the NFL's uniform supplier and holds the same position with the NBA and MLB — but the replica jerseys fans actually buy are made and sold by Fanatics. Nike pays to put its swoosh on garments it neither makes nor sells at retail. The value chain runs backwards from what an apparel company would expect, which only makes sense if impressions rather than units are the product.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike pays to make the jerseys that the players wear. It is a billboard, it is a sponsorship.
You're going to buy a replica from the team store that is made by fanatics that has the Nike swoosh on them.

fragments.title: The banned-shoe story as manufactured myth
fragments.content:
The black-and-red shoes that drew the NBA's letter were modified Airships, not the Air Jordan 1, and there is no footage of Jordan wearing them in a game. What dollars ever changed hands is unknown and may be zero. None of that mattered: the commercial with black bars over the shoes made the ban itself the product story. The story was the asset, and its accuracy was irrelevant.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: To this day, no one can find footage of him wearing the black and red precursor to the Air Jordan 1, these modified airships, on the court.
The thing that's so great, though, is it doesn't matter. It's the story, it's the dream.

fragments.title: Taking a position as media strategy
fragments.content:
The 2018 Kaepernick campaign scrapped a year of planned advertising across every geography and sport. Kaepernick played a sport irrelevant to shoe sales and had not played in years — the campaign was pure halo. It ran two years before George Floyd, when it was still a genuine risk rather than a consensus position. The characterisation offered is that this is executive gut feel about values rather than segment arithmetic.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: believe in something, even if it means sacrificing everything
This actually was a big risk. If this had been done two years later, it would have played out very differently.

fragments.title: The wholesale-to-direct transition, still unfinished
fragments.content:
Roughly 60% of revenue still moves through wholesale, with 40% now direct through owned stores and digital. Four mobile apps carry 500 million users a quarter. But recent quarters reopened Macy's and pushed more inventory into Foot Locker, which raises the question of whether that is strategy or an $8.5 billion inventory problem being discounted through the old channel.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: About 60% is still wholesale, is still sold through retailers.
they have 500 million users a quarter, who are now using Nike digital apps

fragments.title: Innovation arriving from outside the shoe industry
fragments.content:
The waffle sole came from Bowerman pouring polyurethane into his wife's waffle iron, gluing it permanently shut — the iron was found decades later in a rubbish heap and Nike holds it still. Air came from Frank Rudy, a former NASA engineer Knight nearly threw out of his office until Rudy mentioned Adidas had passed. The pattern is that the breakthroughs came from a track coach and an aerospace engineer, not from footwear designers.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: He sees the waffle iron and he's like, what if I pour polyurethane into the waffle iron?
Rudy's like, yeah, Adidas didn't want it either. Phil's like, oh, you said the A word. All right, let me try it.

fragments.title: The Jordan 3 was designed by asking the customer what he wanted
fragments.content:
Tinker Hatfield was trained as an architect, and applied the architect's method: ask the client for specifications. Jordan wanted soft leather needing no break-in, a mid-cut for less weight, and a shoe that worked on court and off. Hatfield delivered exactly that list — plus no swoosh on the side, replaced by the Jumpman. Removing its own logo from its most important shoe is the clearest measure of how little leverage Nike held.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: He goes right down the checklist.
And then the pièce de résistance, no swoosh.

fragments.title: A bad product nearly lost the whole relationship
fragments.content:
The Air Jordan 2 was made in Italy from premium leather at $100 against the AJ1's $65 — stiff, hard to break in, and poor to play basketball in. Combined with Jordan's broken foot and channel stuffing in year one, sales across three years barely exceeded year one alone. The line about Gucci leather captures the failure: the product drifted away from the athlete it was built for.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: The Air Jordan 2s sucked. There's no other way to put it.
Do you want to play basketball in Gucci leather? Probably not.

fragments.title: Year one of Jordan was inflated by stuffing the channel
fragments.content:
Nike sold $126 million of Air Jordan product in year one and about $150 million across three years — the gap explained by pushing product onto retailers through the Futures Program rather than by real demand. True demand was perhaps $50-100 million, still unprecedented. The hangover contributed directly to the year-two collapse. The most celebrated launch in sneaker history was partly a financing manoeuvre.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike needed that first year of the Jordan deal to be a huge hit, so they stuffed the channel.
There wasn't actually $126 million of demand for Jordan products that year.

fragments.title: Breaking2 as a spectacle deliberately outside the rules
fragments.content:
Nike staged a sub-two-hour marathon attempt with rotating pacers and a Tesla projecting a laser pace line — conditions that invalidate a record under competition rules. Nike's position was that this was a stunt and others could argue about legality afterwards. It is the clearest modern expression of the third Nike principle, and it generated far more attention than a sanctioned attempt would have.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: We're just doing a stunt. You guys can debate afterwards if this actually set the world record for the marathon time or not.
Perfect results count, not a perfect process. Break the rules, fight the law.

fragments.title: Digital as relationship infrastructure, learned from a failed product
fragments.content:
Nike+iPod in 2006 was clunky and not commercially successful, but it taught Nike where things were heading, and it arrived because Tim Cook had joined the board. It led to the FuelBand, then to apps, then to a direct relationship with hundreds of millions of customers. It also changed acquisition strategy: away from buying brands like Converse and Cole Haan, toward buying capabilities.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: In 2006, they launched the Nike+iPod, which was not a terribly successful product in the market. But man, did it help Nike understand where the puck is going.
they started acquiring capabilities from a bunch of these other companies to help them make this tech migration

fragments.title: The ability to make an athlete into something larger than an athlete
fragments.content:
The stated capability is imagining athletes as carrying the best of the human spirit, so that they become heroes people listen to. Strasser wrote in 1983 that individual athletes, more than teams, would be the heroes — symbols of risk and winning that ordinary people no longer get to do. Both predate the modern celebrity-athlete economy and describe it precisely.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Individual athletes, even more than teams, will be the heroes. Symbols more and more of what real people can't do anymore, risk and win.
then those athletes would become like the heroes of old, the heroes in books

fragments.title: Scale as the thing an athlete cannot get anywhere else
fragments.content:
The Kobe case is the demonstration: he paid to leave Adidas rather than be paid to stay. The shoe was part of it, but the substance is that what Nike could do for him — and therefore what he could participate in — was exponentially larger. Nike is not simply writing bigger cheques; it is offering a machine no competitor can assemble, which is scale economies expressed through talent.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: I think the issue was what Nike could do for Kobe, and thus what Kobe could participate in, was exponentially higher than even what Adidas could do.
he bought Adidas out of his deal, and then move over to Nike

fragments.title: Ten principles typed in anger, still operative
fragments.content:
Strasser wrote Nike's principles on a typewriter in 1977 and pinned copies around the office — not Phil Knight, not the Nike Corporation yet, and with no swoosh on the document despite what circulates online. Our business is change. We are on offense all the time. Perfect results count, not a perfect process. Live off the land. If we do the right things, we'll make money damn near automatic. They read as strategy, foreshadowing and indictment at once.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: (2) We are on offense all the time.
(10) If we do the right things, we'll make money damn near automatic.

fragments.title: Bowerman's contributions were rare and enormous
fragments.content:
Bowerman appears sporadically and each time changes the company: the nylon-upper Cortez, the jogging book that helped start American fitness, the waffle sole, and coaching Steve Prefontaine at exactly the moment Nike needed a face. He had also written to Adi Dassler in the 1950s trying to buy direct and offer design ideas, and been brushed off — which is why he said yes to Knight instantly.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: His contributions, though sporadic when they happen, are enormous.
Bowerman is sitting there and he is primed. He's like, oh, you're going to import foreign shoes and give me a deal, I'm in.

fragments.title: Scale advantage inside a fragmented factory ecosystem
fragments.content:
Footwear manufacturing is fragmented, but the set of large, fully-audited factories anyone wants to work with is limited. Being the player that can dominate capacity in those factories is a real advantage, distinct from owning any of it. Nike is highly prescriptive — sourcing materials, running audits — without holding the assets.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: being the scale player that can dominate the capacity in those factories is a huge advantage
They're unbelievably prescriptive. They source all the materials. They do lots of audits, stuff like that.

fragments.title: Personalisation at a scale nobody else can reach
fragments.content:
Nike ID, now Nike By Me, lets any customer design their own shoes in their own colours. Doing that for a customer base this size while also producing the standard lines requires scale economies competitors cannot match — the customisation is not a feature so much as another expression of the same underlying advantage.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Anybody can make their own Nike shoes in their own colors with their own designs on them.
that requires a level of scale economies that nobody else can really match

fragments.title: A deeply insular culture that grows its own
fragments.content:
People develop up through Nike and stay for decades — Mark Parker started as a designer and designed the Pegasus, still the longest continuously running model. The competitive culture is absolute: you wear Nike, never a competitor, because that is playing for the other team. That insularity is a strength and is also why the succession bench is thin.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike's also so insular. People develop up through the company and stay there forever.
At Nike, you play to win.

fragments.title: The founding strength became the defining scandal
fragments.content:
Labour arbitrage was not a drift from the plan — it was the Stanford thesis. Child labour, dirt floors, toxic glues and roughly 70 cents a day surfaced in the 1990s, and Nike compounded it by disclaiming responsibility, telling the press it did not make shoes. Mark Parker's later reversal, that ignorance is not bliss, is the correction. The generalisable lesson stated is that a company's greatest strength is also its greatest weakness.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: At the same time, people are making 70¢ a day working in these factories.
They literally said to the press, oh, we don't make shoes.

fragments.title: The betrayal that shaped the culture
fragments.content:
Strasser — architect of the Jordan deal, the college programme and the ten principles — left after a fight, started a consultancy, and became CEO of Adidas America. He died of a heart attack eight months in, aged 46, and Knight did not attend the funeral. Adidas's American headquarters remain in Portland, poaching Nike people to this day. The competitive intensity that built the company also made reconciliation impossible.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: When Rob dies, Phil does not attend his funeral.
From Phil Knight, it might have been okay if he had just quit, but he went to work for Adidas, an intolerable betrayal. I never forgave him.

fragments.title: Winning made them slow
fragments.content:
After the 1980 IPO Knight took a year's sabbatical and the company assumed the running boom would continue. They held roughly 50% of the US running market, which caps growth by arithmetic, and treated a cyclical fad as a secular trend. The diagnosis offered is hubris: for the first time they had capital and were no longer the underdog, and it blinded them to the next market.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: I think it was pure hubris that blinded them from finding their next market.
They 50% market share in running shoes at this point in America

fragments.title: The reorganisation may have traded focus for legibility
fragments.content:
Nike restructured from sport-based teams to men's, women's and kids' — sensible against how retail is actually organised. The risk named is losing the obsessive per-sport focus that built the company, at exactly the moment On, Hoka and Brooks are winning in running trainers by doing precisely that. With running goes Nike, offered as the bellwether.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: what has gotten lost is an obsession and focus on these individual sports and the journeys in the sports.
It's like with running goes Nike, that's a bellwether.

fragments.title: A CEO from outside the shoe business, and a thin bench
fragments.content:
Mark Parker's designated successor was removed amid the me-too and Oregon Project controversies, and John Donahoe arrived from ServiceNow, eBay and Bain — a board member but not a shoe person, in a company where leaders have always risen from inside. The read offered is stabilisation rather than a twenty-year tenure, which leaves succession an open question.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: They're theoretically thin on people who could take the job.
I'm not sure he'll be a 20-year CEO.

fragments.title: China is both the largest opportunity and the least controllable
fragments.content:
A slowdown is affecting all foreign brands, with signs the market is shifting toward Chinese-native labels. Nike's willingness to take public social positions sits awkwardly with operating under the CCP. Since China is the largest market in the world for footwear, whether Nike can address it is described as the question rather than a question.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: It seems like the Chinese market is shifting to Chinese-native brands
Are they going to be able to address that biggest market in the world for feat or not? At scale, it's the question.

fragments.title: Everything rests on continuously repurchased relevance
fragments.content:
With no switching costs, no network effects and no cornered resource, nothing holds a customer between purchases. The business is one where the shoes wear out and the decision is made afresh every time — which is a fine position while the brand leads and an unforgiving one otherwise. Even the durability case rests on brand and scale, not structure.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Unlike tech businesses, there's no potential for any form of lock-in
It's just a thing we need to just keep replacing.

fragments.title: Growth declared as identity
fragments.content:
Nike's investor relations page states that Nike Inc is a growth company, in large letters over an athlete's photograph. It began as a survival requirement under 100% leverage and has become a stated identity — which sits oddly against $10.7 billion of idle cash and thirty quarters of dividend increases. The declaration outlived the condition that produced it.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: If you go to their investor relations page to this day, across the top in big bold letters, it says, Nike Inc is a growth company.
But Nike is a growth company.

fragments.title: Competing to the line and one toe past it
fragments.content:
The pattern recurs: the Mexican factory that ended the Onitsuka relationship, the spy at Onitsuka and the memo announcing it, the secret New Hampshire factory bought with money earmarked for inventory, employing Prefontaine as a public affairs director, Breaking2. The formulation offered is that Nike asks what others assume cannot be done, does it, and handles the consequences afterwards.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: they are competitive all the way up to the line and then one toe over
is there anything we can do that other people aren't doing because they think you can't, but maybe we'll do it anyway and deal with the repercussions?

fragments.title: Standing with the athlete as the durable position
fragments.content:
From circumventing amateurism rules for Prefontaine, through giving Jordan royalty participation nobody else would, to standing by Tiger Woods when others would not — the consistent choice is the athlete's side. It is presented as strategy rather than sentiment: it is what makes the roster available and the brand meaning coherent, and it is the axis on which Nike declined Kanye where Adidas did not.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: And Nike was on the side of the athlete, which is a thing that they've always been, and it's a huge part of their strategy.
We would stand by Tiger Woods, we did in some really trying times in his life, where a lot of people turned against him.

fragments.title: Deliberately giving value away to keep the dream reachable
fragments.content:
Nike lets billions of dollars of resale value flow to StockX, GOAT and individual arbitrageurs, and declines to raise prices even $20 above competitors. The interpretation is that maximum swooshes in the world is worth more than the margin dollars — brand ubiquity purchased with foregone profit. It is a rare case of a company making an obvious, sustained choice to hand value to other players in its own ecosystem.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: They're willing to give margin dollars for that.
I really can't think of anything else off the top of my head where a company is making such an obvious and clear choice to give value to other players in the ecosystem

fragments.title: Betting that scale lets them go direct
fragments.content:
The direct-to-consumer shift is framed as the bet that Nike is one of the few hero brands with enough scale to bypass intermediaries — the Disney analogy, where the scale player can run a playbook unavailable to everyone else, over a ten- to fifteen-year transition. It reverses the wholesale model Knight built with the Futures Program, and it is the largest strategic change in the company's history.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: Nike's basically betting that they're also one of these hero brands that can run that playbook.
There is this tipping point where a brand becomes the scale player.

fragments.title: The unresolved question the company is built on
fragments.content:
Great product or great marketing — the question the episode opens with and never fully settles. Nike does real R&D and has produced genuine breakthroughs, and it also succeeds because it built the best brand, the best distribution and the most affecting advertising. Knight's own answer favours marketing. That the company began by distributing someone else's product is offered as the most telling evidence.

Source: nike.txt (Acquired podcast transcript, Season 13 Episode 1, ~40K words), nike.json (R&D extraction: 11 dimensions, 7 Powers, 8 strategic arguments, Decision Stack)

evidence.text: There's an age-old question in business. What is more important, a great product or great marketing?
I do think it's quite telling that they started distributing someone else's product.
